report.answer_text:
The estimated chance of 2024 YR4 hitting Earth rose to a record in early 2025, then fell to nearly zero within a few days in February.
Late December 2024 to January 2025: The asteroid was found on 27 December 2024. Shortly after discovery, automated warning systems calculated a very small chance of an Earth impact on 22 December 2032.[1] New observations on 29 December 2024 raised the probability, and all three impact monitoring systems rated it Torino Scale level 1.[2]
29 January 2025: ESA put the impact probability at 1.2%[1], and NASA's CNEOS and NEODyS gave consistent independent estimates.[1] The International Asteroid Warning Network (IAWN) issued its first-ever impact notification.
Rise to the peak: At first, the probability rose because a growing share of the asteroid's possible orbits led to an Earth impact.[3] As the range of possible positions narrowed, Earth made up a larger part of it, so the probability increased.[4] NASA reported a 3.1% probability on 18 February[5], while ESA's assessment peaked at 2.8%.[3] ESA said the asteroid held the record for the highest impact probability of any asteroid larger than 30 m, and for the longest time above 1%.[6] It reached a Torino scale rating of 3.[7]
19–20 February: Observations from the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope cut ESA's estimate in half the next day.[3] NASA reduced its figure from 3.1% to 1.5%.[8]
Around 25 February: ESA lowered the probability to 0.001%[3], and the asteroid fell from Level 3 to Level 0 on the Torino scale.[3] NASA's figure was slightly different, about 0.0017%.[4]
After February: The Earth impact has been ruled out, but a roughly 4% probability of a lunar impact on 22 December 2032 remains.[2] A later analysis notes that by the end of the observing period, only a possible 2047 impact remained, with a probability below 10⁻⁵.[2]
The rise and fall followed a pattern scientists expected. As uncertainty shrinks, the probability climbs if Earth stays inside the shrinking range of possible positions. It drops to near zero once Earth falls outside that range.
